analysis.one_liner: Forces agencies to prove rules are least-cost, hold courtroom-style hearings, and survive lawsuits before major rules take effect.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 238-183 in January 2017, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite how federal agencies write rules. Agencies would have to adopt the "least costly" rule that meets a law's goals, hold courtroom-style hearings where company lawyers can cross-examine government scientists for the biggest rules, and let courts re-decide legal questions from scratch instead of deferring to agency experts. Any rule projected to cost the economy $1 billion or more could not take effect until every lawsuit against it was finished. Supporters called this transparency and accountability; its practical effect would be to make new federal safeguards for workers, consumers, and the environment much slower and harder to issue.
analysis.who_benefits: Large corporations in heavily regulated industries — energy, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, finance, manufacturing — would gain the most. The least-cost mandate, the litigation delay for $1 billion rules, courtroom-style hearings, and fresh judicial review all give companies new tools to stall or kill rules they dislike. Law firms that specialize in challenging federal rules would gain a larger market. Small businesses would get expanded impact analyses, input panels run by the Small Business Administration, and outreach requirements, though large regulated firms would be the primary beneficiaries.

how_it_helps.text: Agencies would have to adopt the least costly rule that meets a statute's objectives; a costlier rule is allowed only if the agency proves the extra benefits justify the extra costs — a shift that favors regulated industries over stronger safeguards.

A rule projected to cost the economy $1 billion or more per year could not take effect until every court challenge against it was finally resolved, or until a 60-day review window passed with no one suing — a delay that can run for years.

High-impact rules would require formal hearings where affected companies get a 'reasonable opportunity for cross-examination' of the agency's evidence, turning rulemaking into trials that only well-funded parties can sustain.

Courts reviewing agency actions would have to decide all legal questions 'de novo' — fresh, without deferring to the agency's interpretation of the statutes it administers — giving companies a much better chance of overturning rules in court.

Rules expected to cut employment or wages in an industry by 1% or more would be tagged as 'negative-impact on jobs and wages rules' and face extra notice and documentation requirements before adoption.
The bill exempts the Federal Reserve's monetary policy decisions from the new cost and hearing requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Workers, consumers, patients, and communities that rely on federal safeguards would bear the cost. Rules on workplace safety, clean air and water, drug safety, wages, and consumer finance would take longer to issue, face more lawsuits, and be easier to strike down in court. Agencies would carry heavy new paperwork and hearing burdens, and federal courts would absorb a wave of new challenges. Delay itself is the cost: protections people are counting on arrive years late or not at all.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on federal health and safety rules

drawbacks.text: The bill's transparency measures respond to a real grievance: agencies would have to post a 100-word plain-language summary of each proposed rule, report monthly to the White House regulatory office on upcoming rules, and post required information online for six months before a rule takes effect.

The small-business provisions have genuine substance: expanded regulatory flexibility analyses, review panels convened by the SBA's Chief Counsel for Advocacy, mandatory periodic review of rules affecting small entities, and outreach to small firms owned by women, veterans, and disadvantaged individuals.

The bill lets the president waive the six-month online-posting delay for rules needed because of an imminent threat to health or safety, other emergencies, criminal law enforcement, or national security — so the worst-case delay argument has limits.

A fair objection in the bill's favor: agencies have long used nonbinding 'guidance' documents to shape behavior without full notice-and-comment procedures; the bill would require documented cost-benefit reasoning for major guidance and give affected parties at least 90 days to comply.

An honest supporter would concede the core tradeoff: procedures like cross-examination hearings, litigation holds, and de novo court review do not distinguish good rules from bad ones — they slow and raise the price of every major rule, and the parties best equipped to use them are large corporations, not the public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency and small-business provisions are real but modest; a 100-word summary and monthly reports do not offset the structural changes. The bill's center of gravity — the least-cost mandate, the litigation hold on billion-dollar rules, courtroom-style hearings, and de novo judicial review — would systematically slow and weaken the machinery that produces worker, consumer, and environmental protections. Those procedures are cheapest to exploit for the largest regulated companies. On balance, the costs to the public's protections would outweigh the accountability gains, and the bill's design points that way deliberately.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House on a near-party-line vote two weeks into the new Congress, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Goodlatte introduced the bill on January 3, 2017, the first day of the new Congress, and it was referred to the Judiciary, Oversight, and Small Business Committees.

On January 11, 2017, the House debated the bill under a rule from the Rules Committee, considered more than a dozen amendments, and rejected a Democratic motion to recommit that would have exempted rules lowering prescription drug costs for seniors on Medicare Part D, by a vote of 190-233.
The House passed the bill that same day, 238-183, with 233 of 240 Republicans voting yes and 183 of 194 voting Democrats voting no; only 5 Democrats crossed over.

The Senate received the bill on January 12, 2017, and referred it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee; the Small Business Committee held a hearing on March 29, 2017, but no committee or floor vote ever followed.
The bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, having never received a Senate vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who depend on federal health, safety, wage, and financial protections are better off, because the machinery for issuing those rules was not rewired. The business coalition that pushed the bill gained nothing from its death.

for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for the bill as their top regulatory priority at the start of the Trump administration.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost perfectly by party: 233 of 240 Republicans voted yes, while 183 of 194 voting Democrats voted no, with only 5 Democrats in favor.

industries.industry: Regulated corporations (energy, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, finance, manufacturing)
industries.note: The bill hands these companies the least-cost mandate, litigation holds on billion-dollar rules, cross-examination hearings, and fresh judicial review — all tools for delaying or killing rules they face. Their gain comes directly at the expense of the timeliness and strength of public protections.

industries.industry: Law firms specializing in challenges to federal rules
industries.note: De novo review of all legal questions, immediate review of interim rules, and formal hearing procedures would open many more avenues to sue over agency rules. More litigation means more billable work, and the delay it produces falls on the public.

The bill expands regulatory flexibility analyses, requires review panels and outreach to small firms, and lets the SBA's Chief Counsel weigh in on rulemakings. These provisions could genuinely reduce compliance burdens on small firms, though the bill's biggest beneficiaries would be large regulated corporations.
